articles.title: The Wait for a First Action, by Technology
articles.content:
by Dennis Crouch

In my post on Monday, I created a time series chart showing the average/median wait time for utility patent applications from filing to the first action on the merits. But, that office-wide average hides some major differences across technology areas.  For this post, I broke out the data for the past three months by technology family as shown in the chart below.

The dashed line on the chart marks 14 months -- the benchmark in the patent term adjustment statute. The solid line is the all-family average, about 20 months on this measure.

The 33 technology families are my own groupings. I created them to keep the number of groups manageable, combining art units that appear to share similarities in both technology and prosecution process.  I also have a table at the end of the post that lists the art units in each family.

articles.title: Design Patent Infringement Test Heads Toward the Supreme Court
articles.content:
by Dennis Crouch
Range of Motion Products, LLC v. Armaid Co., No. 26A564 (U.S. 2026)
I have been following Range of Motion v. Armaid since before the Federal Circuit's divided panel decision in February. Range of Motion Prods., LLC v. Armaid Co., 166 F.4th 981 (Fed. Cir. 2026). The design patent case is now starting its Supreme Court journey. Most recently, Chief Justice Roberts granted the patentee's unopposed application for a 42-day extension -- making its petition for certiorari due December 21, 2026. Noted IP-focused Supreme Court counsel Joshua Rosenkranz (Orrick) is handling the case on behalf of the patentee.
Your lawyering professor likely taught that every court filing provides an opportunity to make your case. This includes applications for extending a filing deadline. The application filed here previews two questions. The first is whether the "plainly dissimilar" noninfringement shortcut from Egyptian Goddess, Inc. v. Swisa, Inc., 543 F.3d 665 (Fed. Cir. 2008) (en banc), conflicts with the "substantially the same" test that the Supreme Court set out in Gorham Co. v. White, 81 U.S. 511 (1871). The second asks whether judges may resolve factual disputes over which features of a design are functional as part of claim construction -- or whether that is a question for the jury.
Range of Motion contends that leaving those disputes to the judge conflicts with the Seventh Amendment jury right and with Markman v. Westview Instruments, Inc., 517 U.S. 370 (1996). Both questions divided the Federal Circuit. When the court denied rehearing en banc in August, Chief Judge Moore dissented, joined by Judge Reyna, and Judges Stoll and Stark dissented without opinion.

articles.title: Revived and Forgotten: Should This Patent Issue?
articles.content:
by Dennis Crouch

I have been looking at patent applications that appear to be lost within the USPTO digital files. A common pattern is abandonment, followed by revival on petition, but then the file is apparently forgotten about for years. In many cases the PTO's internal docket flag remained abandoned.

This post takes a closer look at one of those files: U.S. Application No. 13/734,654, filed by IBM in 2013 and owned by Lenovo since 2014.

The application was allowed in December 2014, but the issue fee was not paid on time. In October 2015, the USPTO granted a petition to revive (the fee came with the petition) and sent the file off to be printed as a patent. Eleven years later, it still has not issued. Meanwhile, the patent term adjustment clock continues to run. If the Office printed it now, the patent would expire around 2044 rather than 2033 - more than a decade after its own continuation.

Question for you: Should this patent issue? Or should we blame the applicant for eleven years of silence?

articles.title: The Wait for a First Action
articles.content:
by Dennis Crouch

The wait for a first action on the merits (FAOM) has eased a bit over the past year, but the numbers are still about seven months over target. Most recently, the average application waited about 21 months from filing to receive an action. That is down from about 24 months at the peak, and still well above the 16 months of 2020.

The chart below tracks the average by month mailed (a trailing three-month average) for utility applications in the USPTO's public file-wrapper data. The dashed line is the USPTO's own dashboard figure. Mine runs about half a month higher because the USPTO counts a restriction requirement as stopping the clock.

articles.title: Issue Fee to Grant: The Wait Has Doubled
articles.content:
by Dennis Crouch
I recently received a question from a practitioner about how long patents are now taking to issue after the issue fee is paid. The short answer is about twice as long as this spring. For utility patents issued in the first half of 2026, the median wait from payment to grant was 29 days. For patents issued September 1 through October 20, the median was 60 days, with almost no patents issuing within four weeks of the fee-payment.
The irony is that the delay appears to come from an efficiency gain. Early this year, the USPTO reworked how it handles notices of allowance, cutting processing time from 25 minutes per application to 6. In April, the Office used that new speed to clear its backlog of allowance notices -- mailing about 17,000 in a single week, roughly two and a half times the usual number. Applicants have three months to pay the issue fee, and the payments arrived in a July (heat) wave. But the speed-up in one part of the system was then slowed down by another part. In particular, the problem appears to be that the Office of Patent Publication was not prepared for the influx. That group kept issuing about 6,000 utility patents a week, and the pile of paid-but-unissued applications grew from its usual ~28k to a peak of ~54k in early October. It now stands at about 51k and appears to be slowly shrinking.
And, the Office has stepped up the number of patents being readied for issue each week -- now issuing over 7,000 per week. But, even at the stepped up pace, the queue probably won't fully clear until early 2027.
